stem: A private manufacturer (not a public business entity) leases its plant from an LLC owned by the same shareholder, under a signed three-page agreement. May it use the practical expedient in 842-10-15-3A to determine whether the arrangement is a lease?

choices.text: Yes — it is an eligible entity with written terms for a common control arrangement, and it need not assess enforceability
No — the expedient is only for arrangements between unrelated parties
Yes — but only after obtaining a legal opinion that the agreement is enforceable
No — arrangements between commonly controlled entities are never leases

feedback: Everything lines up: the entity is not a public business entity, a not-for-profit conduit bond obligor, or an SEC-filing employee benefit plan; the arrangement is between entities under common control; and written terms exist. The expedient then asks only whether those written terms convey the practical right to control the use of the identified asset. Answer (b) inverts the scope — common control is the expedient's whole subject; (c) reinstates the enforceability assessment the expedient exists to remove; (d) confuses hard-to-assess with nonexistent. Re-study block 2 (S-02, the expedient).

stem: Why did the FASB conclude that legal enforceability was a poor basis for lease accounting between entities under common control?

choices.text: Assessing it could require a costly legal opinion, while the common owner could amend or decline to enforce the terms at any time
Common control arrangements are always unwritten, so there is nothing to enforce
Courts refuse to hear disputes between related parties
Enforceability only matters for finance leases

feedback: The Board's Basis for Conclusions records both halves: determining enforceable terms of a common control arrangement could necessitate a formal legal opinion — challenging and costly precisely because of the common control — and the common owner typically can amend, or simply not enforce, the terms at will, making enforceability a strange foundation for the accounting. Answer (b) overstates — many such arrangements are written, and the problem persisted even then; (c) invents a legal rule the Board never relied on; (d) has no basis — enforceability went to whether a lease existed at all. Re-study block 3 (S-03, why the Board moved).

stem: A commonly controlled lessee makes leasehold improvements with a twelve-year useful life to the common control group, under a four-year lease. Over what period does it amortize the improvements?

choices.text: Twelve years — the useful life to the group — for as long as it controls the use of the asset through a lease
Four years — the lease term always caps amortization
The shorter of the two, as for any leasehold improvement
Twelve years, unconditionally — control of the asset is irrelevant

feedback: 842-20-35-12A displaces the general rule for common control leases: the improvements amortize over their useful life to the common control group, regardless of the lease term, as long as the lessee controls the use of the underlying asset through a lease. Answers (b) and (c) apply the general 35-12 rule that this paragraph specifically overrides; (d) drops the condition that does the work — lose control, and the remaining balance transfers instead of amortizing on. Re-study block 4 (S-04, the roof rule).
_source: sources/asc842/842-20-35-12A.txt; sources/asc842/ASU_2023-01.txt para 9 (35-12 general rule shown as amended)

stem: A commonly controlled lessee vacates the leased building, ceasing to control its use, while its leasehold improvements still carry an unamortized balance. What happens to that balance?

choices.text: It is accounted for as a transfer between entities under common control, through an adjustment to equity
It is written off as a loss in earnings
It continues to amortize over the remaining useful life
Prior-year statements are restated as if the shorter life had been used

feedback: When the lessee no longer controls the use of the underlying asset, 842-20-35-12A(b) treats the remaining improvements as a transfer within the common control group — an equity adjustment, reflecting value moved from one commonly controlled pocket to another rather than value destroyed. Answer (b) is the earnings hit the Board specifically rejected as unrepresentative; (c) keeps amortizing an asset the lessee no longer benefits from, ignoring the condition; (d) makes retrospective what the standard treats as an event of the period. Re-study block 5 (S-05, when control ends).

stem: An operating company uses its sibling entity's warehouse under an entirely unwritten arrangement. Can it apply the written-terms practical expedient?

choices.text: No — with no written terms, it must apply the general guidance and its enforceable-terms analysis
Yes — oral terms qualify if both entities confirm them
Yes — the expedient assumes a lease exists whenever entities are under common control
No — and no lease can exist without a written agreement

feedback: 842-10-15-3B is categorical: if no written terms or conditions exist, the expedient is unavailable, and the entity determines whether a lease exists — and classifies it — from the legally enforceable terms. The practical answer is to write the arrangement down; at transition the Board expressly permitted documenting existing unwritten terms before the first statements applying the expedient were issued. Answer (b) is what 'written' rules out; (c) mistakes an evidence shortcut for a presumption; (d) overcorrects — an unwritten arrangement can still be (or contain) a lease under the general guidance. Re-study block 2 (S-02) and block 6 (S-06, transition).
_source: sources/asc842/ASU_2023-01.txt para 4 (842-10-15-3B) and Summary/BC47 (documenting unwritten terms at transition)

stem: Which entity may NOT elect the written-terms practical expedient in 842-10-15-3A for its common control arrangements?

choices.text: A not-for-profit entity that is a conduit bond obligor for exchange-traded securities
A privately held manufacturer
A not-for-profit entity that is not a conduit bond obligor
An employee benefit plan that does not file financial statements with the SEC

feedback: The expedient excludes three kinds of entity: public business entities, not-for-profit conduit bond obligors, and employee benefit plans that file or furnish financial statements with the SEC. A conduit bond obligor NFP is therefore out, while ordinary private companies (b), other NFPs (c), and non-filing benefit plans (d) are in. If (a) surprised you, you may be carrying over lesson 2's scope — the risk-free rate election does admit conduit bond obligors, because its only test is not being a public business entity. The two lists differ, and this is where. Re-study block 2 (S-02, who is eligible).
_source: sources/asc842/842-10-15-3A.txt; sources/asc842/ASU_2023-01.txt Summary ('available to entities that are not…')

stem: Under the practical expedient, an entity determines whether a lease exists by asking whether the written terms and conditions convey what?

choices.text: The practical — as opposed to enforceable — right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration
A legally enforceable right to use the asset, confirmed by counsel
An intent by both parties to be bound indefinitely
Ownership of the underlying asset

feedback: That is the expedient's exact substitution: the lease test still asks about control of an identified asset for a period in exchange for consideration, but the right need only be practical, not enforceable, and it is read off the written terms. Answer (b) restores the enforceability inquiry — and the legal opinions — the expedient removes; (c) swaps the control test for a vague mutual-intent test found nowhere in the guidance; (d) confuses leasing with owning — a lease conveys use, not the asset. Re-study block 2 (S-02, the expedient).
_source: sources/asc842/842-10-15-3A.txt ('practical (as opposed to enforceable) right to control')

stem: Which statement about the leasehold-improvements amendment in ASU 2023-01 (842-20-35-12A) is correct?

choices.text: It applies to all lessees in common control leases — public business entities included — not only to entities eligible for the written-terms expedient
It applies only to entities that have elected the written-terms practical expedient
It lets any lessee, related or not, amortize improvements past the lease term
It exempts common control leasehold improvements from impairment testing

feedback: The ASU's two issues have two scopes: the written-terms expedient is limited to private entities, but the leasehold-improvements accounting applies to every lessee in a common control lease, public companies among them. Answer (b) welds the two issues together — no election is involved in 35-12A, it is a requirement; (c) extends the rule beyond common control, where the shorter-of rule in 35-12 still governs; (d) reverses 35-12B, which specifically keeps Topic 360 impairment testing in force. Re-study block 4 (S-04, the reach of the rule).
_source: sources/asc842/ASU_2023-01.txt Summary (Issue 2 affects all entities); sources/asc842/842-20-35-12A.txt; ASU_2023-01.txt para 9 (35-12B)

stem: A commonly controlled lessee amortizes its leasehold improvements over a fifteen-year useful life to the group under a five-year lease. What must it disclose while that mismatch exists?

choices.text: The unamortized balance of the improvements, their remaining useful life to the group, and the remaining lease term
Nothing — related party disclosures under Topic 850 cover it
Only the fact that the practical expedient was elected
A pro forma income statement as if the lease term had been used

feedback: When the useful life to the common control group exceeds the related lease term, 842-20-50-7A requires exactly those three numbers, so the reader can see the mismatch the accounting is deliberately carrying. Answer (b) treats general related party disclosure as a substitute for a specific requirement layered on top of it; (c) reaches for the wrong amendment — the improvements accounting is not an expedient election at all; (d) invents a pro forma requirement the Board never proposed. Re-study block 6 (S-06, the disclosure).
